thread.title: Nissan's Premium Brand Infiniti Stalled In The U.S. This Year: What's The Outlook? - Nissan Motor Co., Ltd. ADR (OTCMKTS:NSANY)

author: Anton Wahlman
title: Nissan's Premium Brand Infiniti Stalled In The U.S. This Year: What's The Outlook? - Nissan Motor Co., Ltd. ADR (OTCMKTS:NSANY)
text:
Infiniti had a weak start to 2018, as measured by U.S. unit sales: Here.
U.S. unit sales for Nissan's ( OTCPK:NSANY ) premium vehicle division are down 8.3% for the first four months of 2018. What's happening under the surface at Infiniti in the U.S. market?
At 49,847 units sold in the U.S. in the first four months of 2018, things would superficially be on track for approximately 150,000 units sold in 2018, which is close to the 153,415 sold in 2017 and reasonably above the 138,293 number for 2016. However, the 8.3% year-to-date decline indicates that not all is well. The purpose of this report is to analyze the situation on a nameplate by nameplate basis, including my observations from having driven the Infiniti vehicles in question.
I had the opportunity to spend anywhere between one and five days each behind the wheel of almost all of Infiniti's current lineup of vehicles - cars and crossover SUVs. The two exceptions were its largest sedan, the Q70, which comes in standard and long wheelbase versions, and the QX70 crossover, which is being discontinued after the current season anyway.
With the Q70 being so small, volume wise, and the QX70 going away this year, the six Infiniti nameplates I drove constitute 95% of Infiniti's volume in the U.S. market:
QX50 - midsize crossover
QX30 - small crossover
QX60 - large SUV-crossover
QX80 - large SUV
Q50 - compact sedan
Q60 - coupe
So let's discuss the market trends for these nameplates in turn:
QX50 midsize crossover
There are two good reasons I'm starting with the QX50. While it is only 11% of U.S. unit sales in the first four months of 2018, far behind the QX60, Q50 and even the QX80, it is underperforming dramatically inside the Infiniti portfolio, when compared with similar vehicles inside other automaker portfolios. Among almost all of Infiniti's competitors, this segment participant is the brand best seller in most instances. That goes for BMW, Mercedes, Audi, Volvo, Cadillac, Lexus and Jaguar, among others.
The reasons the QX50 is so important going forward are twofold:
As I mentioned above, this is the body style that usually sells more units than all the others. In some cases, it is as high as 25% to 50% of a premium brand's sales. It is almost a given that with this new model that went on sale in late 1Q 2018, it will at least double sales, up from the current 11% contribution.
The QX50 is also the Nissan Group's launch vehicle for its variable compression gasoline engine. This is an industry-first - an engine that varies its stroke by a few millimeters in order to generate a compression ratio spanning from 8:1 when driven aggressively, to 14:1 when driven gently.
The QX50 starts at $37,545. Mechanically, it only comes with one engine and transmission. You have a choice between front wheel drive and all-wheel drive - plus the trim level and relatively few options after that.
But let's talk about those trim and options packages, and how much they add to the base price. The Sensory package alone is $7,500, and the Autograph package is $2,000. The car I drove had those things, and more. Once you have added all the options (not including accessories such as rubber floor mats and equivalent), you arrive at $58,995. That's a big jump from the $37,545 base price - but it's still the same engine.
With that having been pointed out, in this highest trim and with all the options, we see a whole new level of interior material ideas from Infiniti. The first thing that strikes you is the blue suede and the contrast to the other materials and colors. I can't recall anything quite like this blue suede anywhere near this price point. It looks and feels special.
Those interior materials and colors come off very well. This is a fresh idea.
However, not all is well with the QX50 interior. Some of the interior panels surrounding the center stack come together in ways that I could best describe as "visual noise." It just doesn't look right. It's not a manufacturing quality issue at all, as that's impeccable on all Infiniti models. It's strictly a design consistency issue, fitting the shapes together. You really have to see it to understand.
The other thing that is ugly is the most objective weak point of the QX50: The infotainment system. It lacks Android (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) Auto and Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) CarPlay, which is a no-no in today's market.
But it gets worse. The embedded system, including its maps, are simply the worst. The fonts are in the direction of a 1980s Atari and spells "very dated" - which is not a good thing in anything that's supposed to spell "computer" and "modernity." I think Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA ) does the best job in terms of creating a modern "style" of its screen, even though I'm not a fan of Tesla's lack of buttons and knobs. I want both, but most of all I want Android Auto and Apple CarPlay.
Driver comfort is pretty good, average for this premium class - seat, seating position and related. I still think the segment leader here is the Audi Q5 followed by the Volvo XC60. Rear seat space is excellent for the class.
Driving the QX50, it's a mostly very good experience. The revolutionary new engine has a distinct "bite" to it. It feels solid. I can't wait to see this engine make itself into the rest of the Nissan and Infiniti lineups. Eventually, to Mitsubishi and Renault too.
The transmission is a CVT, which I am one of the seemingly few to like - in general. However, in this application, it has been designed so as to fake non-existent shifts. This forfeits the whole purpose of a CVT, in my opinion. Let the CVT be a CVT. Its charm is its step-less rubber band operation - not faking non-existent shifts.
Taking all of those things into consideration, the driving experience of the QX50 can best be described as neutral. It doesn't stand out materially in either way in this premium segment. It's a good experience, but so are most of the competitors.
What stands out, at least on paper, is the class-leading fuel economy, for a non-diesel, non-hybrid vehicle. In all-wheel drive, it yields an average of 26 MPG. Front-wheel drive only yields 27 MPG. In my brief time with the car, I was unable to confirm this number - in part because I drove the car much more aggressively than I would normally do. I look forward to spending more time with this car, in a setting where I can draw some more accurate fuel economy conclusions on my own.

As you can see in the table above, U.S. sales of the QX50 started to improve when the all-new QX50 arrived near the end of March 2018. I predict that sales will improve further in the months to come. Based on how the equivalent models do inside the other automakers, the QX50 has the capacity to at least double this year.
As for the car itself, the verdict from what I discussed above is that the QX50 has one major weakness and one major strength. The weakness is the infotainment system, and the strength is the all-new revolutionary variable-compression engine.
QX30 compact crossover I drove the QX30 for a few days and it was a bit of a doozy. The thing I like the most about the QX30 is its styling. It is basically a Volkswagen ( OTCPK:VLKAY ) ( OTCPK:VLKAF ) Golf type of a hatchback, but it looks very good, especially from the rear and from the rear profile. Very similar to the Mazda 3, it looks a lot wider than it is.
The QX30 was in part jointly developed with Mercedes. It's basically the Mercedes GLA under the skin. The instrumentation seems completely taken from Mercedes, making it different from other Infinitis. The engine is built by Nissan in the U.S. and the car is assembled in the U.K.
Aside from the perennial Infiniti infotainment problem, the other "problem" with the QX30 is that it does not stand out in any particular way. I failed to see any compelling reason to recommend it, other than the excellent exterior styling.
In any case, the QX30 started U.S. sales in the middle of 2016 and became a huge success for Infiniti for one year. Then, in the second half of 2017 sales started to decline. So far in 2018, sales are down 55%. Sales are barely higher than the Q60 coupe!
Compact crossover is a booming segment in general, so the QX30 being down 55% is a massive underperformance. It's a major headwind to Infiniti's U.S. sales this year.
QX60 - midsize-large crossover-SUV The QX60 is Infiniti's best-selling vehicle in the U.S., and it's also the only Infiniti built in the U.S. It's really no surprise, given that it was in many ways Infiniti's breakthrough product in this market.
The QX60 is a very American product. It's spacious and soft. It was one of the first unibody three-row SUVs. It offends nobody, and has a lot of utility.
After driving it for a few days, I found the QX60 to be dated. The dashboard looks a decade old, and the infotainment system is - you guessed it - terrible. There's no Android Auto or Apple CarPlay.
My other pet peeve with the QX60 is that it has many reflective materials on and around the center stack that blind the driver when the sun shines from a particular angle. The QX60 is not the only offender in the auto industry on this point, but it's problematic.
In 2018, QX60 sales are up 31.4% in the U.S. This makes it the best Infiniti performer in the U.S. this year. The best explanation for this is that the QX60 continues to fit the U.S. consumer tastes so well right now, in terms of offering a great interior space combined with a soft and pleasant ride.
QX80 - large SUV For the U.S. market - as well for the Arabic Gulf states - the QX80 is Infiniti's crown jewel. It's basically the same car as the Nissan Armada, but with air suspension and a nicer interior.
But before we get to the interior, let's first recognize why the Infiniti QX80 has been such an enduring sales success in the U.S. market: Exterior styling. It's a very majestic vehicle. Chief Designer Alfonso Albaisa referred to it as "Baroque." I couldn't agree more. You buy the QX80 because you want to feel like king of… something.
The interior also is great looking. The diamond-quilted brown leather is stunning. The first impression here is very strong.
However, I don't like the driver's seat comfort. The seat is too flat and slippery. Furthermore, the infotainment controls are as bad as they are in the other Infiniti models. It needs a totally new system, which would have Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. There also are shiny materials around the center stack that blind the driver, just like in the QX60.
All that said, the QX80, despite its size and considerable weight, doesn't feel as large as it is. It does feel heavy. If you want to feel like you're driving a tank, the QX80 is for you. It's more American than a Cadillac (NYSE: GM ) Escalade in that regard.
The fuel economy is miserable. Tooling around town, it was a challenge to exceed 13 MPG. On the highway, I had a hard time getting to 18 MPG.
I really want to love the QX80. It looks so great and is so totally in-your-face. It's an emotional thing. However, the utility and technology are not competitive. My favorite in this class is the Ford (NYSE: F ) Expedition, which doesn't look as good, but is better at almost everything else.
Sales of the QX80 are down 2.6% in the U.S. this year, but from a very elevated level. The annualized sales level of around 20,000 is very good. This is a vehicle for which one is very much rooting.
Q60 - coupe The Q60 is the coupe version of the Q50 compact sedan. It is immediately recognizable because of its differentiated exterior styling. It is not confused with anything else in the market.
The Q60 is rear wheel drive based, but has optional all-wheel drive. With up to 400 horsepower available, it is very much a car that begs to be driven aggressively. This is a car for burnouts and drifts. Turn off the traction control and floor it! You will have a lot of fun.
The interior is OK - except for the infotainment system, which lacks Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. As with the other newest Infiniti models, the interior design is reasonably elegant and feels like quality.
From a sales perspective, 2018 has been a down year. The 20.9% decline, however, comes on the back of a huge sales increase last year, and the current absolute level of sales runs around 10,000 per year in the U.S. That's actually a very large number for a coupe of this nature and price range.
Q50 - compact sedan There really isn't all that much to say about the Q50 sedan that doesn't also apply to the Q60 coupe discussed above. It lacks the coupe's great exterior looks, but doesn't look bad. The interior and all other traits are essentially the same.
From a sales perspective, the Q50 has its heritage in being the second-oldest Infiniti volume model and is the second best-selling Infiniti now. Sales are up 4.4% in 2018. The Q50 got a mild refresh in August 2017, in order to align it with the Q60 which arrived in the market one year prior. The various trim levels are now essentially the same as they are for the coupe.
Conclusion: What's next for Infiniti? Infiniti's U.S. 8.3% decline in 2018 is the result of the QX30 underperformance, the aging small-volume Q70's decline, and the QX70 going away. The major improvement has come from the QX60, which is actually a vehicle that's long in the tooth - but fits the current U.S. market needs very well.
For the near term, the focus should be on the QX50, which is where Infiniti has the greatest market potential, and should easily be able to double in 2018 and into 2019. Furthermore, this revolutionary new variable-compression engine should find itself into other Infiniti models soon. Nissan already announced it for the midsize Altima sedan, which arrives this fall.
It will probably take at least two years, perhaps three, until all Infiniti models get some version of this new variable-compression engine by 2021. This will be phased in with refreshes and all-new models.
Then, just as that transition has been completed, in 2021, Infiniti's electric drivetrain era begins. That's when we will see the first of multiple all-electric Infiniti models.
Infiniti is to Nissan what Lincoln is to Ford. It isn't going away. To the contrary, it's growing.
Disclosure: I am/we are short TSLA.
Additional disclosure: At the time of submitting this article for publication, the author was short TSLA and long GM and GOOGL. However, positions can change at any time. The author regularly attends press conferences, new vehicle launches and equivalent, hosted by most major automakers. Infiniti and Nissan hosted product launch events.
